The southern viscacha Lagidium viscacia exhibits a suite of life-history traits characteristic of high-altitude, herbivorous rodents adapted to the rocky outcrops of the Andes. Neonates emerge after a gestation period that falls within a relatively narrow range, with field data indicating a duration of 134 days [tg = 134 days] when measured at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This protracted gestation, which aligns with reports of 120 to 135 days in the literature, is typical of larger caviomorph rodents and likely reflects the advanced state of development of the precocial young at birth. Correspondingly, newborn individuals have a wet weight at birth of 260 grams [Wwb = 260 grams], a substantial mass that equips the pups for the cold and rugged environment they must navigate shortly after parturition. This combination of a long intrauterine development and a large neonatal mass represents a significant maternal investment.

Reproductive output in Lagidium viscacia is constrained by its extended gestation and the demands of a harsh, seasonal environment. Females typically produce 1.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1.5 pups per litter], a modest litter size that aligns with the species’ K-selected life-history strategy. Under the stable thermal conditions of typical body temperature, which is 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the maximum annual reproductive rate is estimated at approximately one litter per year [F_R_i = approximately one litter per year], leading to a relatively low yearly output of offspring. Consequently, the maximum reproduction rate for this species reaches approximately 1.5 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 1.5 offspring per year]. This reproductive pace is consistent with that of other chinchillid rodents and reflects the energetic constraints of lactation and pup rearing in an environment where food resources are patchy and seasonal. The trade-off between offspring size and number is heavily skewed toward producing a small number of highly developed young.

Growth and development in the southern viscacha proceed through clearly defined ontogenetic stages. At a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the neonatal period is relatively brief, and weaning occurs at 56 days since birth [tx = 56 days since birth]. At this point, the young are nutritionally independent, though they often remain within the natal colony for an extended period. The trajectory toward reproductive maturity is considerably longer, with females reaching puberty at 258 days since birth [tp = 258 days since birth] under the same thermal conditions at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This delayed sexual maturation, spanning over eight months, allows for substantial somatic growth and the accumulation of skeletal mass necessary to support future pregnancies. The interval between weaning and puberty represents a critical phase of juvenile development.

Adult body size in Lagidium viscacia is comparatively large for a chinchillid, with individuals ultimately attaining a wet weight of 3000 grams [Wwi = 3000 grams]. This substantial adult mass is supported by a correspondingly high basal metabolic rate. Respirometry trials conducted at a standard body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] have recorded a maximum basal oxygen consumption of 699 milliliters per hour [JOi = 699 milliliters per hour], a value that reflects the energetic demands of thermoregulation and maintenance in a cold, hypoxic environment. This metabolic rate is considerable when scaled against body mass, suggesting a high cost of living that is supported by a diet of tough, fibrous grasses. The integration of large body size with a heightened metabolism is a hallmark of species inhabiting productive, albeit seasonal, high-altitude grasslands.

Longevity in the southern viscacha is remarkable among rodents of its size, reflecting a slow-paced life history. Captive and field records indicate a maximum lifespan of 19.5 years [am = 19.5 years], with this value documented at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This extended lifespan, equivalent to over seven thousand days, is a striking feature that aligns with the species’ delayed maturation, low fecundity, and well-developed anti-predator behaviors, including retreat into rocky crevices. The annual probability of mortality is consequently low among adults. This suite of life-history attributes—large body mass, high investment per offspring, slow development, and extreme longevity—places Lagidium viscacia at the slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum, similar to other long-lived, high-altitude specialists.
